Smart Cities Dive reports that the original rowhouse was built in 1847 and converted as part of a subway vent fan plan in 1908.The building is one of New York’s most unusual examples of infrastructure hidden in plain sight. More than a century after the subway company bought and gutted it, the facade continues to protect a piece of transit engineering that helps keep the tunnels below safe for passengers. Read more details about it here, as per the report:In 1907, the Brooklyn Rapid Transit Company purchased the 1847 townhouse at 58 Joralemon Street. Rather than demolishing it completely, the company gutted the interior and converted it into a ventilation structure for the subway tunnels running beneath the East River.The conversion was part of a broader plan to supply fresh air to the subway system. A 1906 letter from the chief subway tunnel engineer, published in The City Record, explained that vents were needed in both Manhattan and Brooklyn to maintain an adequate air supply and keep the East River tunnels safe for public use.The plan called for exhaust grates at a shaft near a new high-pressure pumping station at the foot of Joralemon Street. A cross-section illustration published at the time showed the subway beneath the river and the ventilation shafts connected to it, the report suggested.The decision to preserve the building’s exterior was practical as well as aesthetic. Brooklyn Heights was already an established residential neighbourhood, and a large industrial ventilation structure would have stood out sharply among its historic rowhouses.By retaining the brownstone facade, engineers created a structure that looked familiar from the street while concealing a deep shaft and emergency stairway below. The result was a piece of transit infrastructure that could exist without visibly disrupting the character of the surrounding block.The building’s windows are permanently blacked out, a detail that hints at its unusual purpose. From the outside, however, it still reads as a historic townhouse rather than an obvious subway facility.Contemporary newspaper reports show the scale of the work. Articles from The Daily Eagle in July 1907 described the ventilation shaft as nearing completion, alongside a corresponding vent on the Manhattan side.Photographs from the period show a gaping hole extending roughly five storeys below ground level, while neighbouring homes remained untouched. The construction required removing the townhouse’s interior while preserving enough of its exterior to maintain the appearance of an ordinary residence.The shaft connects to the subway tunnels under the East River, allowing air to move through the system. It also provides an emergency exit stairway, giving the structure a second critical safety function beyond ventilation.The building has not remained unchanged since its early-20th-century conversion. The New York Transit Museum told Smart Cities Dive that the structure was renovated in 1999, with upgrades to the decades-old ventilation machinery and improvements to the facade.That renovation helped modernise the equipment while preserving the building’s historic-looking exterior. It also ensured that the ventilation system could continue supporting the subway infrastructure beneath the East River.The project shows how cities often maintain old infrastructure by layering new technology into existing structures. Rather than replacing the entire facility, the transit agency upgraded the machinery and restored the facade, allowing the building to continue serving its original purpose.The building is well known to historians and nearby residents, but the Metropolitan Transportation Authority has generally kept it low-profile. A 2004 report in The New York Times said the agency preferred to keep the site “incognito for security reasons.”Despite that caution, the “Shaft House” has become an open secret among neighbours. Its unusual blacked-out windows and its role in subway operations have made it a recurring subject of curiosity for locals and urban-history enthusiasts.The secrecy is understandable. The building contains operational transit infrastructure, including a ventilation system and emergency exit route. Keeping attention away from its interior helps protect both the equipment and the safety function it performs.New York’s Joralemon Street building is part of a longer tradition of disguising transit infrastructure as ordinary buildings. In London, the facades at 23 and 24 Leinster Gardens appear to be typical townhouses, but closer inspection reveals painted-on windows and doors without handles.Those London facades were created after the original homes were demolished for an underground railway route that opened in 1868. They conceal a subway vent and were designed to help the infrastructure blend into a prestigious residential street.Paris has a similar example at 145 Rue Lafayette, where a false-fronted home serves as a subway ventilation chimney. In each case, engineers faced the same challenge: essential infrastructure needed to be located in a dense urban neighbourhood without overwhelming its visual character.The Brooklyn building is more than a curiosity. It demonstrates how transit systems depend on infrastructure that most passengers never see, including ventilation shafts, emergency exits, tunnels, and air-management systems.It also shows how historic architecture and modern infrastructure can coexist. The 1847 facade gives the building a place in the neighbourhood’s streetscape, while the interior has served the subway system for more than a century.For anyone walking past 58 Joralemon Street, the lesson is simple: not every building is what it appears to be. Behind one of Brooklyn’s most convincing facades lies a working piece of subway history that still helps keep the tunnels below safe.
Article Summary: 58 Joralemon Street was built in 1847 and converted as part of a subway vent fan plan in 1908. The company gutted the interior and converted it into a ventilation structure for the subway tunnels running beneath the East River. By retaining the brownstone facade, engineers created a structure that looked familiar from the street while concealing a deep shaft and emergency stairway.

Article Title: Texas approved a reservoir that could flood more than 16,000 acres of ranchland; after years of landowner opposition, a judge has overturned the permit, though Wichita Falls can still appeal
Article Text:
Why the Lake Ringgold project faced opposition

Judge overturns the reservoir permit

Wichita Falls keeps its options open

A wider debate over water security and property rights

Poll Vote & Share your view What should be prioritized when considering projects like Lake Ringgold? Water supply needs Agricultural land protection Environmental conservation Community input 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A Texas judge has overturned a state-issued permit for the proposed Lake Ringgold reservoir, handing a significant victory to ranchers and conservation groups that have spent years challenging the project. The ruling, delivered by Travis County District Judge Maya Guerra Gamble on October 8, 2026, puts a major obstacle in the path of a reservoir intended to strengthen water supplies for Wichita Falls and the surrounding region. According to reporting by KAUZ News Channel 6 and statements from the Texas & Southwestern Cattle Raisers Association and Texas Conservation Alliance, the proposed project in Clay County could inundate more than 16,000 acres of agricultural land and wildlife habitat. The City of Wichita Falls, however, has indicated that it remains committed to the reservoir and has the option to appeal the decision.The proposed reservoir has been promoted as a long-term solution to water security concerns in North Texas, where drought and growing demand have intensified the need for reliable supplies. City officials have argued that developing additional water resources is essential to preparing the region for future shortages.For ranchers and conservationists, however, the project’s potential costs extend well beyond the construction of a new reservoir. The planned lake could submerge productive grazing land, disrupt established ranching operations and permanently transform parts of the Little Wichita River corridor.The Texas Conservation Alliance has also raised concerns about the loss of native tallgrass prairie and wildlife habitat. Opponents argue that a project of this scale must be supported by a clear demonstration of water demand and a thorough assessment of alternative ways to meet it. Landowners challenged the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality’s approval of the reservoir permit, seeking judicial review of the decision and the justification for the project.The latest ruling reverses the environmental regulator’s earlier decision to issue the permit, marking a major development in the long-running dispute. The Texas & Southwestern Cattle Raisers Association welcomed the outcome, describing it as an important milestone for private property rights and the protection of agricultural land. The association had supported affected landowners throughout the legal process.Texas Conservation Alliance also backed the challenge, arguing that responsible water planning must balance future supply requirements with environmental protection and the interests of people whose livelihoods depend on the land. The ruling does not necessarily end the Lake Ringgold proposal. Instead, it leaves the project facing a legal setback that could delay its progress while the city considers its next steps.Wichita Falls has maintained that Lake Ringgold remains an important part of its long-term water strategy. Following the ruling, Mayor Tim Short told KAUZ that the city had 30 days to appeal and would discuss how to proceed over the coming weeks. The city’s public works director, Russell Schreiber, also indicated that the latest development was one stage in a longer permitting and construction process. Officials continue to point to the drought conditions that initially prompted the proposal as a reason to pursue additional water infrastructure. An appeal could prolong the dispute, leaving landowners uncertain about the future of their properties and the city facing further delays in its efforts to secure water supplies.The Lake Ringgold case reflects a recurring challenge in Texas: how to expand water infrastructure while protecting private land, agricultural livelihoods and ecologically sensitive areas.Reservoirs can provide important safeguards against drought, but large projects can also require substantial land acquisition and alter landscapes for generations. For affected ranchers, the potential loss of thousands of acres raises questions about the long-term consequences of prioritising water storage over existing land uses.The legal challenge has placed those competing interests under scrutiny, with landowners arguing that the need for additional water must be weighed against the project’s environmental and economic costs. For now, Judge Gamble’s decision has halted the permit’s progress. Whether the ruling ultimately ends the Lake Ringgold proposal or leads to another round of litigation will depend on the city’s next move and the legal proceedings that follow
Article Summary: A Texas judge has overturned a state-issued permit for the proposed Lake Ringgold reservoir. The ruling puts a major obstacle in the path of a reservoir intended to strengthen water supplies for Wichita Falls and the surrounding region. The City of Wichita Falls, however, has indicated that it remains committed to the reservoir.

Article Title: A former luxury steam yacht sank off San Francisco in 1920; researchers brought back the first underwater images using underwater robots
Article Text:
PC: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Office of National Marine Sanctuaries

How did the luxury steam yacht Ituna sink off San Francisco

What was the Ituna before it became a commercial fishing vessel

PC: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Office of National Marine Sanctuaries

Sonar technology helped identify the Ituna shipwreck off California

How many shipwrecks lie beneath the Greater Farallones National Marine Sanctuary

The Ituna was built in 1886 as a luxury steam yacht and was lost in 1920 while working as a steam trawler. A gale struck north of the San Francisco Lightship station on 13 March 1920, and the 34-year-old vessel sank in 10 minutes. Twelve of the 14 crew members escaped, and two did not. According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Office of National Marine Sanctuaries, sonar expert Gary Fabian has since used a remotely operated vehicle and an autonomous underwater vehicle to bring back what NOAA describes as the first underwater images of the shipwreck.The Ituna was heading from San Francisco to Reedsport, Oregon, when the storm struck on 13 March 1920. The agency states that the seas split the ship's seams and flooded the forward hold, which plunged the vessel bow-first to the bottom of the ocean. The sinking took only 10 minutes.12 of the 14 crew members escaped and struggled for hours to keep their lifeboat afloat on the journey to the San Francisco Lightship. Two crew members were trapped in their bunks and went down with the ship. The vessel's cargo of machinery, bound for the Reedsport Fish Company, was valued at $30,000 at the time.NOAA states that the Ituna began life as a luxury steam yacht, built for John G. Mackie in 1886 by A. & J. Inglis in Glasgow, Scotland. It was named for the Latin name of the Solway Firth, the coastline border between England and Scotland. After several changes of ownership, it was bought by Allison V. Amour of Chicago, Illinois, whom NOAA describes as a wealthy socialite interested in natural sciences. In December 1894, the Ituna left New York for Havana and Mexico on a three-month scientific research expedition. The results were published as Archaeological Studies Among the Ancient Cities of Mexico, which scholars of Mesoamerican anthropology valued immensely.The vessel later became a first-class passenger cargo steamer, running between ports along the United States West Coast and Mexican ports under the flag of the Mexican Navigation and Commercial Company. Two years after that, it was purchased by the Frank E. Booth Canning Company of San Francisco and converted into a seagoing steam trawler. According to NOAA, it was one of the largest steam trawlers fishing off California's central coast and one of the first commercial fishing vessels to introduce the "otter trawl" to the Pacific coast, in 1918.Its Office of National Marine Sanctuaries Maritime Heritage Program worked in partnership with Teledyne SeaBotix, Inc. and sonar expert Gary Fabian. The team used a remotely operated vehicle and an autonomous underwater vehicle to collect high-definition video footage, still images and side-scan sonar data for analysis. NOAA credits Cyril Poissonnett of Teledyne SeaBotix with deploying the autonomous underwater vehicle for the side-scan sonar survey of the Ituna.The images show the vessel's steel hull, which was designed by the yacht designer George Lennox Watson, as well as its triple expansion steam engine and its cargo of machinery. The agency reports that the clipper-ship bow of the former yacht provided identification of the wreck. NOAA adds that multiple marine species have colonised the shipwreck, including giant green anemones (Anthopleura xanthogrammica) and white plumose anemones (Metridium farcimen).Nearly 400 ships and aircraft wrecks lie on the seafloor of the recently expanded Greater Farallones National Marine Sanctuary and the nearby Golden Gate National Recreation Area, including four never-before-found vessels. The Maritime Heritage Program is engaged in a two-year study to discover and document these wrecks. 20 ships have been plotted so far, including the USS Independence and the freighter S.S. Selja.NOAA quotes Robert Schwemmer, West Coast Regional Maritime Heritage Coordinator, as saying the Ituna's story is an example of "the rich maritime legacy that rests beneath the waves of San Francisco Bay." Schwemmer also states that mapping and examining the wrecks is a key part of preserving them for future generations. He says exploration allows researchers to learn about the past of the United States as a seafaring nation and to test recent advances in technology that will help protect these marine resources.
Article Summary: The Ituna was built in 1886 as a luxury steam yacht and was lost in 1920 while working as a steam trawler. A gale struck north of the San Francisco Lightship station on 13 March 1920, and the 34-year-old vessel sank in 10 minutes. Twelve of the 14 crew members escaped, and two did not. Sonar expert Gary Fabian used a remotely operated vehicle and an autonomous underwater vehicle to bring back what NOAA describes as the first underwater images of the shipwreck.

Article Title: OpenAI faces lawsuits from 8 US states over ChatGPT’s alleged harm to users
Article Text:
lawsuits accuse OpenAI of violating state consumer protection laws by misleading users about ChatGPT’s safety

States seek changes to ChatGPT

OpenAI faces growing legal challenges

OpenAI is facing a fresh legal challenge in the US, with attorneys general from eight states accusing the company of exposing users, including teenagers, to harmful behaviour through its ChatGPT chatbot. The lawsuits allege that the AI tool has reinforced delusions, encouraged self-harm and helped users plan violence, including mass shootings.Attorneys general from Iowa, Kansas, Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho, Montana, Nebraska and West Virginia filed separate lawsuits in state courts on Wednesday. The complaints claim ChatGPT is designed to be agreeable and engaging to build users’ trust, potentially making them more vulnerable to dangerous interactions.The lawsuits accuse OpenAI of violating state consumer protection laws by misleading users about ChatGPT’s safety. They also allege that the company has created a public nuisance by endangering the health and safety of residents.The states are seeking court orders requiring OpenAI to change how ChatGPT operates. Among their demands is a prohibition on developing AI models capable of improving themselves unless the company can ensure that the models are aligned with human values.The states are also seeking civil monetary penalties for alleged violations of state laws, along with damages.The coordinated legal action adds to mounting legal scrutiny of OpenAI as the company prepares for a potential public listing. It represents a significant coordinated effort by state authorities to challenge the safety of an AI company’s products.Florida’s attorney general filed the first lawsuit of its kind by a US state against OpenAI in June, citing concerns over child safety.The company is also facing dozens of lawsuits brought by private plaintiffs alleging that ChatGPT contributed to harmful behaviour, including helping users plan mass shootings and other acts of violence.
Article Summary: States seek changes to ChatGPT. OpenAI faces growing legal challenges in the US. Lawsuits allege that the AI tool has reinforced delusions, encouraged self-harm and helped users plan violence, including mass shootings. Florida’s attorney general filed the first lawsuit of its kind by a US state against OpenAI in June.

Article Title: Conservationists spent years making repeated attempts to protect Tennessee’s Devil’s Racetrack; a $2.45 million deal has finally secured 350 acres for a state park and the Cumberland Trail
Article Text:
A multi-year effort to protect one of the Cumberland Trail’s most significant and distinctive landscapes has reached a major milestone with the acquisition of approximately 350 acres at Devil’s Racetrack. Image Credit: The Nature Conservancy

Importance of the Devil’s Racetrack land acquisition for Tennessee’s Cumberland Trail

The Cumberland Trail. Image Credit: Mark Engler/Tennessee River Valley

A distinctive landscape receives long-term protection

The finish line at Devil's Racetrack. Image Credit: Mark Engler/Tennessee River Valley

How was the $2.45 million purchase funded

The Cumberland Trail gains ground through sustained cooperation

Tennessee has secured approximately 350 acres at Devil’s Racetrack through a $2.45 million land acquisition, bringing years of conservation efforts to a significant milestone. The purchase protects one of the Cumberland Plateau’s most distinctive geological landscapes and creates new opportunities for the continued development of the Cumberland Trail. Announced on 23 September 2026, the deal brings together public funding, private contributions and sustained advocacy to safeguard the area for future generations. The newly acquired land will be managed by Justin P. Wilson Cumberland Trail State Park as plans for its future take shape.The acquisition marks an important step towards protecting Devil’s Racetrack, a rugged natural formation recognised for its unusual rock features and dramatic terrain. Situated on the Cumberland Plateau, the landscape forms part of a wider natural area that gives the Cumberland Trail much of its distinctive character.According to The Nature Conservancy , the purchase follows multiple attempts over several years to secure the property.Conservationists and supporters had worked towards protecting the site, but turning that goal into reality required sustained planning, fundraising and cooperation between different organisations.FOX 17 News reported that the $2.45 million transaction was completed to preserve the land for the trail’s future development. The agreement means the property can now be incorporated into the broader conservation and recreational vision for the region.Devil’s Racetrack is particularly notable for its exposed rock formations and striking natural contours. These features reflect the rugged character of the Cumberland Plateau, where rocky ridges and steep terrain help define the landscape.The Nature Conservancy explains that protecting the property is important not only because of its appearance but also because of its natural and recreational value. Securing the land provides a stronger foundation for keeping these features intact while allowing future generations to experience the area.The purchase also helps protect the setting in which the Cumberland Trail will continue to develop. Rather than treating the site simply as another section of land, the acquisition preserves a distinctive part of Tennessee’s natural heritage.FOX 17 News reported that state and conservation partners are looking towards future public access and trail development. However, the acquisition itself represents the securing of the property, with further planning still to come.The transaction relied on a combination of public money and private conservation support. According to The Nature Conservancy’s announcement, the organisation contributed $500,000 towards the acquisition and covered the costs of the property appraisal, a Phase I environmental study and a survey.The remaining purchase costs were funded through Tennessee’s State Lands Acquisition Fund. This arrangement brought together financial assistance and practical support, helping the state complete a deal that had required years of preparation.The Nature Conservancy’s contribution extended beyond its direct financial commitment. Covering the appraisal, environmental study and survey also helped meet the technical requirements involved in securing the property.The Nature Conservancy also acknowledged the role of state officials and long-standing trail supporters in helping advance the project. Its Tennessee State Director, Laurel Creech, credited the persistence of the conservation community and the use of both public and private funding for making the acquisition possible.The Devil’s Racetrack purchase forms part of a much wider effort to complete and protect the Cumberland Trail, Tennessee’s flagship backcountry hiking route. Among those recognised by The Nature Conservancy is Justin P. Wilson, a former Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation commissioner and Tennessee comptroller emeritus. His long-standing commitment to the trail, alongside philanthropic support, has helped sustain the broader vision for its development. Conservation groups can contribute funding, expertise and advocacy, while state agencies can provide resources and oversee the management of protected land.With ownership secured, attention can turn towards planning the land’s future role in the Cumberland Trail. The Nature Conservancy confirmed that the newly protected acreage will become part of the trail’s continued development and will be managed by Justin P. Wilson Cumberland Trail State Park.
Article Summary: Tennessee has secured approximately 350 acres at Devil's Racetrack through a $2.45 million land acquisition. The purchase protects one of the Cumberland Plateau’s most distinctive geological landscapes. The newly acquired land will be managed by Justin P. Wilson Cumberland Trail State Park as plans for its future take shape.

Article Title: Trump defends Qatar's 747 gift as he hits campaign trail ahead of US midterms
Article Text:
“When you’re given gifts, you take ’em, right?” Trump told supporters in Bullhead City, Arizona. “When they give you a 747 you say two words: ‘thank you.’”

Trump brushes aside affordability concerns

US President Donald Trump defended his acceptance of a luxury Boeing 747 gifted by Qatar during a campaign rally in Arizona on Wednesday, saying that when someone gives you a gift, the appropriate response is to say thank you. Trump later travelled to Montana as part of a Western campaign swing aimed at boosting Republican candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.“When you’re given gifts, you take ’em, right?” Trump told supporters in Bullhead City, Arizona. “When they give you a 747 you say two words: ‘thank you.’”Trump recounted how he learnt that Qatar had one of the best Boeing 747 aircraft and called the country's emir to ask if he could borrow it. According to Trump, the emir offered the aircraft as a gift instead. His acceptance of the luxury jet last year drew criticism, including from some of his staunchest Republican supporters.The president’s remarks came as rising living costs remain a major concern for Americans ahead of the midterm elections. While candidates across the country are increasingly focusing on economic pressures facing voters, Trump devoted much of his Arizona speech to the aircraft and his plans for renovations in Washington.Trump spoke about the White House ballroom under construction, a newly completed helipad on the South Lawn and a proposed triumphal arch in the US capital.“The fake news media doesn't talk about how well we're doing” as a country, Trump said, adding that journalists instead questioned him about “affordability” in what appeared to be a dismissive reference to the issue.The rally was held in Bullhead City in Mohave County, an area with higher poverty and unemployment rates and lower per-capita income than Arizona and the US overall, according to census and state unemployment data.Trump's visits to Arizona and Montana followed campaign stops in Alaska on Tuesday and Ohio on Monday. White House press secretary Katie Zacharia described the series of rallies as a “midterm blitz”, as Republicans attempt to limit expected losses in elections that will determine control of Congress.Arizona is the only swing state among Trump's recent campaign stops. Although Trump won the state in 2016 and 2024, he lost it in 2020.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump defended his acceptance of a luxury Boeing 747 gifted by Qatar during a campaign rally in Arizona on Wednesday. Trump later travelled to Montana as part of a Western campaign swing aimed at boosting Republican candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

Article Title: Pakistan regulator warns TV channels against live coverage of blasts and terror attacks
Article Text:
The regulator also stressed the need for stronger editorial oversight.

Channels told to air only verified information

Legal action for violations

Pakistan's media regulator has warned satellite television channels against broadcasting live footage of explosions, gunfire and terrorist attacks, cautioning that violations could lead to legal action.The Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) issued a notification on Tuesday, reminding broadcasters of restrictions first introduced on February 20, 2023. The rules bar news, current affairs and regional-language channels from broadcasting, rebroadcasting or providing live coverage of such incidents.The directive comes as emergency rule has been imposed in the north-western province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, renewing debate over how the media should report security incidents while ensuring that the public receives timely and reliable information.PEMRA has instructed broadcasters to air only “verified information warranted by the relevant government departments or law enforcement agencies”.The regulator also stressed the need for stronger editorial oversight and the effective use of broadcast delays to prevent the immediate transmission of sensitive footage during security incidents.It directed television channels to establish independent editorial boards in line with applicable laws and relevant court judgments.The notification referred to the Supreme Court's judgment in Suo Motu Case No. 28 of 2018 and an Islamabad High Court order dated September 5, 2022, both concerning the prescribed procedure for broadcast delays.PEMRA warned that channels violating the directive could face legal proceedings under Sections 29A, 30 and 33 of the PEMRA Ordinance, 2002, as amended.The latest notification reiterates the regulator's existing restrictions on live coverage of security incidents, with a focus on verification, editorial checks and the use of broadcast delays.
Article Summary: Pakistan's media regulator has warned satellite television channels against broadcasting live footage of explosions, gunfire and terrorist attacks. The Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) issued a notification on Tuesday. The rules bar news, current affairs and regional-language channels from broadcasting or providing live coverage of such incidents.

Article Title: Why Asim Munir's plan to 'split' up Pakistan may spell the end of civilian govt
Article Text:
Asim Munir’s plan to redraw Pakistan: A blow to Sharifs, Bhuttos and civilian power?

Smaller provinces, bigger control? The power game behind Asim Munir’s Pakistan plan

The divide-and-rule calculation

Would breaking up provinces weaken political dynasties?

Punjab and Sindh: The biggest political stakes

The mineral wealth behind the debate

From Balochistan to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa: Mapping Pakistan’s mineral wealth

Why Khyber Pakhtunkhwa could be a test case

Is Pakistan's provincial system failing?

Pakistan is world's fifth-largest country in population

Can Munir get the plan through?

The general vs the dynasties: Who holds the real power in Pakistan?

What happens next?

One military chief, powerful political families: The contest shaping Pakistan

In Pakistan, the prime minister has the title, the president has the office, but the military chief has the power. Now, field marshal Asim Munir, the country's most powerful man, is reportedly considering a way to redraw Pakistan's political map.According to The Economist, Munir is considering a radical solution to Pakistan's governance problems: Breaking up the country's four provinces into 12 to 15 smaller provinces, or possibly reorganising administration into as many as 160 smaller units.Smaller units, according to the argument for restructuring, would be easier to govern. But in a country where the military has long wielded influence over civilian governments, the political question is whether they would also be easier to control.The proposal has also raised concerns that weakening provincial governments could shift more political influence from Islamabad's civilian leadership towards the military establishment in Rawalpindi.However, the plan remains unconfirmed, and its details are unclear. But dividing Punjab and Sindh, strongholds of powerful political dynasties, could weaken established parties.Restructuring Pakistan's political map could also change who controls the country's mineral wealth and other natural resources.The Economist has raised the possibility that the proposal could become a 'divide and rule' exercise, weakening regional power centres and making them easier for the military-backed federal government to manage.Pakistan's population and resources are unevenly distributed, and many regions remain poorly served by their governments.Smaller administrative units could bring officials closer to citizens, improve public services and give neglected areas a stronger political voice.The question is whether the changes would make government more accountable to ordinary Pakistanis or concentrate more power in the hands of Munir and the military establishment.Pakistan's four provinces are Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) and Balochistan. Each has its own elected assembly and provincial government, giving regional parties an institutional base from which to challenge decisions taken by the federal government.Their populations vary sharply. According to the 2023 census, Punjab has around 128 million people, slightly more than half of Pakistan's population, while Balochistan has approximately 15 million, or about 6% of the national total.Punjab's size makes administration difficult, and residents in remote rural areas can spend hours travelling to government offices to settle land disputes or access basic services.But dividing the provinces would have political consequences as well. Large provinces can sustain powerful leaders, substantial bureaucracies and networks of elected representatives with influence beyond individual districts. Breaking them into smaller units could fragment that influence.The military establishment could then be dealing with a greater number of provincial leaders, each with a smaller political base and potentially fewer resources to challenge decisions made in Islamabad.The outcome would not necessarily favour the centre in every case. New provinces could give regional leaders and communities that feel excluded from existing political networks a stronger voice. Much would depend on the powers, funding and autonomy granted to the new administrations.Still, the proposal raises a difficult question: Is Pakistan considering smaller provinces because its existing ones are too large to govern effectively, or because some have become too politically powerful to manage easily?Punjab and Sindh are likely to be at the centre of any serious attempt to redraw Pakistan's provincial map. Both are major political strongholds, and dividing them could change the country's balance of power.Punjab is the main base of the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N), associated with the Sharif family.Nawaz Sharif has served as prime minister, his brother Shehbaz Sharif currently heads the federal government, and Nawaz's daughter Maryam Nawaz is Punjab's chief minister. The family and its party have dominated provincial politics for much of the past four decades.One longstanding proposal is to create a separate South Punjab province. Supporters argue that the region has not received adequate political representation or public investment compared with more developed parts of Punjab. A separate province could focus more directly on local infrastructure, education, healthcare and employment.But dividing Punjab could also break up the Sharif family-led PML-N's large electoral and organisational base, creating new political battlegrounds for regional parties and local leaders.Sindh presents a different challenge. It is the principal stronghold of the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), whose political roots go back to Zulfikar Ali Bhutto. The party has remained under the influence of his family, including his daughter Benazir Bhutto's widower, Asif Ali Zardari, now Pakistan's president, and their son and party chairman Bilawal Bhutto Zardari.Karachi, the country's commercial capital, is also in Sindh and central to its economic and political importance. For the PPP, dividing the province could weaken its established networks.For many Sindhi groups, however, the issue goes beyond party politics: Sindh represents a distinct historical, cultural and linguistic identity.Opposition to the proposal is already clear. On September 4, the Sindh assembly passed a resolution rejecting attempts to divide the province or create administrative units that would alter its boundaries. Chief minister Syed Murad Ali Shah said there would be no compromise on Sindh's geographical unity, Dawn reported.Resistance continued in October. According to Dawn, a multiparty conference held on October 11, attended by representatives of the PPP, PML-N and other political groups, resolved to oppose attempts to create new provinces or administrative units in Sindh.Any attempt to divide the province could therefore trigger a wider confrontation over political power, identity and provincial autonomy.Pakistan's natural resources add another dimension to the proposed restructuring.Balochistan has deposits of copper, gold, chromite, coal and iron ore. Sindh has coal, limestone, silica sand and other industrial minerals, while KP has gemstones, marble, granite, gypsum and other deposits. Punjab is known for rock salt, iron ore, limestone and fire clay. PoK's Gilgit-Baltistan and other areas of Pakistan-occupied Kashmir also have deposits of precious and semi-precious stones and other minerals.These resources have long been at the centre of disputes over mining rights, royalties, investment and the distribution of economic benefits. Provincial governments and local communities have sought a greater say in decisions affecting their land and livelihoods.The proposed restructuring has also raised concerns that weakening provincial governments could give the military-backed federal establishment greater freedom to pursue mineral extraction projects in resource-rich regions without facing the same level of resistance from local authorities.These concerns have not been independently established as Munir's motives. Nor has a detailed plan been made public showing how a new provincial structure would change control over minerals or the distribution of revenues.The concern, however, is clear. A provincial government can negotiate with Islamabad over mining projects, royalties and development spending. A smaller unit with limited revenue and greater dependence on federal funding could find it harder to resist pressure from the centre.Balochistan illustrates the sensitivity of the issue, with long-running disputes over who benefits from the province's mineral wealth and how much local communities gain from projects in their region.Mineral extraction and investment are not, by themselves, evidence of a political power grab. The key question is whether decisions would be made transparently, with meaningful local participation, or imposed by a powerful centre with limited accountability.Developments in Imran Khan's party stronghold Khyber Pakhtunkhwa have added to concerns about the military's influence over provincial affairs.On October 11, President Asif Ali Zardari declared a state of emergency in the province, imposing Governor's rule and effectively suspending the elected government led by Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), the party founded by jailed former prime minister Imran Khan.The Shehbaz Sharif-led government cited rising militant violence and the provincial administration's alleged failure to control the security situation.Imran-led PTI rejected the move, calling it an attack on its political stronghold and accusing the federal establishment of undermining an elected government.Reuters reported that the emergency was accompanied by the appointment of a new governor and the deployment of troops, amid political tensions over a planned march to Islamabad demanding Khan's release. PTI has denied supporting militancy and disputed the Sharif government's account of its handling of the security situation.KP is a key centre of PTI's political influence. Suspending its government has changed the balance between Khan's party and the Islamabad administration.Imran Khan's prolonged imprisonment and the imposition of emergency rule in KP could also be viewed in the context of Asim Munir's long-standing tensions with the former prime minister, who also led Pakistan to its Cricket World Cup victory.However, the emergency does not establish that Munir intends to divide KP or use it as a model for restructuring other provinces. It has nevertheless raised concerns about the federal government's ability to override elected provincial authorities, including in decisions affecting resource-rich regions.Similar concerns have been raised about the possibility of greater federal intervention in Balochistan and Sindh. But there is no established evidence of a coordinated plan to impose such measures across provinces.The argument for smaller provinces has a basis in the governance challenges Pakistan faces. Its population has grown substantially since 1947, while the current four-province structure has remained in place since 1970. Administering a province as populous as Punjab is a major task, particularly when public services remain inadequate in many areas.Interior minister Mohsin Naqvi has argued that the country's governance system has "collapsed" and that the existing structure cannot adequately manage population growth, debt and other pressures. He has called for smaller administrative units as part of wider reforms.But new boundaries alone would not solve corruption, weak public services or economic mismanagement. Smaller provinces would need their own institutions, budgets and administrative staff. Without adequate funding and clear powers, creating new units could increase the cost of government without improving people's lives.The military's own role in Pakistan's governance problems is also part of this debate. The country has spent long periods under direct army rule, and the armed forces continue to wield considerable influence over security and foreign policy, even under civilian governments.In recent months, Munir has wielded extraordinary power, from visiting Washington and cultivating ties with Donald Trump to earning the US president's "favourite field marshal" label and attempting to broker a deal over the Iran war.Under his tenure, Pakistan's army chief has expanded his influence well beyond military affairs, playing an increasingly prominent role in the country's foreign policy.The Economist has argued that the military cannot be separated from Pakistan's governance problems, pointing to its share of public resources, landholdings and commercial interests, as well as its influence over civilian administrations.Pakistan's economic difficulties have several causes, including debt, inflation, weak investment and structural problems in public finances. But the military's political and economic position remains a central issue in debates over accountability and the allocation of resources.Munir's authority has grown against this backdrop. Reuters reported on October 8 that the military had taken on a larger role in foreign and defence policy, including a decision to deploy additional troops to Saudi Arabia under a defence arrangement without parliamentary approval.If provincial governments are weakened while the military's influence grows, critics fear there could be fewer institutions capable of challenging decisions made by the centre. At the same time, smaller provinces could create opportunities for new regional leaders, depending on how much independence they are given.The key issue is not simply the size of the provinces, but who would control their budgets, appointments and natural resources after any restructuring.Even if the military and civilian leadership agree on restructuring, Pakistan's Constitution presents a major hurdle.Article 239 requires a constitutional amendment to secure a two-thirds majority of the total membership of each house of parliament. If an amendment changes a province's boundaries, it must also be approved by the concerned provincial assembly by at least two-thirds of its total membership before it can be presented to the president for assent.That makes dividing Punjab or Sindh politically difficult. The PML-N may have reasons to consider a separate South Punjab province, but splitting Punjab could weaken the Sharif family's political base.The PPP, meanwhile, has repeatedly rejected proposals to divide Sindh, its strongest provincial stronghold.The Sindh assembly's September resolution and the multiparty conference reported by Dawn in October show that opposition extends beyond a single party. Any attempt to alter the province's boundaries without political consensus could provoke a wider confrontation.Balochistan remains a major challenge for the Sharif-Munir duo, with separatist sentiment, demands for greater autonomy and sustained militant activity complicating Islamabad's efforts to assert control over the province.Senator and former Imran Khan ally Faisal Vawda has suggested, in reporting by The Economist, that a referendum could be held in the coming months. But such a proposal raises questions about the legal process and whether a referendum could replace the constitutionally required approvals.There is also a distinction between creating 12 to 15 provinces and establishing as many as 160 administrative units.The first would fundamentally change Pakistan's federal structure. The second could involve districts or other administrative divisions, depending on their legal status and powers.Until a detailed plan is announced, it remains unclear which model is actually being considered.Pakistan's debate over new provinces brings together several long-running disputes: The balance between civilian and military power, the influence of regional political dynasties, and control over natural resources.Supporters argue that smaller provinces could improve governance and give neglected regions a stronger voice. Critics fear that dividing established political strongholds would weaken regional parties and leave provincial governments more dependent on Islamabad.The constitutional hurdles are substantial, and opposition in Sindh is already organised. Developments in KP have added to concerns about the centre's willingness to override provincial authority in the name of security.Pakistan faces serious governance challenges, but whether redrawing its map would address them is another matter. Smaller provinces could help address regional inequalities if they receive adequate resources, meaningful autonomy and accountable institutions.If the changes instead weaken elected governments while concentrating control over funding and natural resources in the centre, the promised benefits may never reach ordinary citizens.
Article Summary: Asim Munir, Pakistan's most powerful man, is reportedly considering a way to redraw Pakistan's political map. He is considering breaking up the country's four provinces into 12 to 15 smaller provinces, or reorganising administration into as many as 160 smaller units. But dividing Punjab and Sindh, strongholds of powerful political dynasties, could weaken established parties.

Article Title: 6 killed, several injured as passenger train derails in Pakistan's Punjab
Article Text:
Train travelling from Karachi to Peshawar derails in Pakistan (Representative image) (PTI)

Poll Vote & Share your view What should be the top priority to prevent train accidents? Improving railway tracks Upgrading safety systems Regular maintenance and inspections 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

At least six people were killed and several others injured after a passenger train derailed in Pakistan's Punjab province early Tuesday, Pakistan-based Geo News reported.The Rehman Baba Express, travelling from the southern port city of Karachi to the northwestern city of Peshawar, derailed in Sher Shah, Punjab province, news agency AP reported, citing Pakistan Railways spokesperson Kaleem Akhtar.The injured were taken to Nishtar Hospital in Multan for treatment, while rescue teams continued operations at the accident site.The accident took place at around 5.15am, according to Geo News.Pakistan President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed grief over the deaths in separate statements and directed authorities to ensure the best possible medical care for the injured.Train accidents are relatively common in Pakistan, where the railway system has suffered from decades of underinvestment, outdated tracks and ageing signalling systems.In 2023, 10 carriages of a passenger train derailed in southern Pakistan, killing 30 people and injuring more than 90 others.
Article Summary: Passenger train travelling from Karachi to Peshawar derails in Pakistan. At least six people killed and several others injured in Sher Shah, Punjab province. Pakistan President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif express grief over the deaths.

Article Title: 2 Pakistan army pilots killed as training aircraft crashes near Balochistan's Quetta
Article Text:
2 Pakistan army pilots killed (IANS photo)

Two Pakistan army pilots were killed after a Mushshak training aircraft crashed near Balochistan's Quetta on Monday due to a technical fault, as Dawn reported, citing the ISPR, the official media wing of the Pakistan armed forces.The Pakistan army identified the deceased as Major Husnain Shehzad Humayun, an instructor, and Captain Abdul Samad, a trainee pilot.The aircraft crashed near Nawan Killi in Quetta.In June, a Mi-17 helicopter belonging to the Pakistan army's aviation wing crashed during take-off near Muzaffarabad in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK), reportedly due to a technical fault.All personnel on board were killed. The ISPR said rescue and recovery teams were rushed to the site and an inquiry was ordered to determine the cause of the crash, Dawn reported.In September last year, five crew members died when a Pakistan army helicopter crashed in the Diamer district of Pakistan-occupied Gilgit-Baltistan (PoGB). The ISPR said the helicopter had encountered a technical fault.In August 2025, five crew members were also killed when a Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government helicopter carrying flood relief supplies crashed in a tribal district, Pakistan-based daily The Express Tribune reported.
Article Summary: Pakistan army identifies the deceased as Major Husnain Shehzad Humayun, an instructor, and Captain Abdul Samad, a trainee pilot. The aircraft crashed near Nawan Killi in Quetta. In June, a Mi-17 helicopter belonging to the Pakistan army's aviation wing crashed during take-off in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.

Article Title: Laiba Ijaz suicide: Pakistan gold medalist commits suicide after visa scam; suspect on 5-day remand
Article Text:
20-year-old physics gold medallist committed suicide after allegedly being scammed of Pakistani Rs 93 lakh over promise of getting an admission in Harvard

Family alleges loss of Pakistani Rs 9.3 million

What FIR alleges

A 20-year-old Pakistani student, Laiba Ijaz, died by suicide on October 9 after allegedly being defrauded of millions of rupees by an agent who promised to secure her admission to Harvard University, a scholarship and a US visa. An Islamabad court on Monday granted police five days of physical remand of the main accused, Muhammad Noman, in connection with the case, Voice PK reported.Judicial magistrate Zunaira Zafar passed the order after police produced Noman in court with his face covered. Police had sought 10 days of remand to investigate his alleged role, verify evidence and examine witness statements.Pakistan's Senate Standing Committee on Human Rights has also sought a detailed inquiry into Laiba's death and the alleged fraud. According to police reporting, the committee will meet on October 15. Islamabad's inspector general of police, the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) director general and the Higher Education Commission chairman have been directed to attend.The committee has sought details of the case registration, the suspect's arrest and the investigation so far. It has also asked authorities to report on steps taken to cancel the licence of the educational consultant accused of issuing fake documents.According to local reports, Laiba was found hanging from a tree in Islamabad's Sector G-10 on Friday, October 9. Police said she had paid an agent Rs 5 million to arrange her travel to the United States but was later given fake documents.Laiba had left home around 2pm, telling her mother she would return shortly. When she failed to come back, her family searched for her and tracked her location using her mobile phone. They found her body and informed the police, who took it to a hospital.The Media Line reported that Laiba was a physics gold medallist and scholarship holder who aspired to become a scientist and study at Harvard. Her family allegedly lost Rs 9.3 million, approximately $34,000, to those promising her admission, a scholarship and a US visa.Her father had sold milk and yoghurt on Islamabad's streets since 1994 to support his family's education. To finance Laiba's studies abroad, he reportedly sold land intended for the family's home, while her mother pawned her jewellery. Laiba had also declined a scholarship in Saudi Arabia because she wanted to pursue her ambitions in the United States.Shortly before her death, Laiba called her brother-in-law and said, "Don't tell my father about the fraud committed against me; otherwise, he will die."Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has ordered an investigation into the case.According to the police FIR, Laiba's father said the family had met Noman around six to seven months before her death. Noman allegedly introduced himself as a senior official in Islamabad and offered to arrange a US study visa for Laiba for Rs 9.3 million.The father alleged that he paid Rs 2.1 million in cash to Noman at G-10 Markaz in the presence of witnesses. Laiba transferred another Rs 2.9 million through her mobile and bank accounts, according to the complaint.Noman allegedly supplied documents that later turned out to be fake. He also reportedly presented a forged receipt showing a transfer of $20,000 into Laiba's bank account to help prepare a bank statement. The father said Noman stopped answering his calls after the family questioned him about the documents.The father also accused a woman identified as Fatima Sarwar, alias Aiza, of involvement in the alleged fraud. She reportedly contacted Laiba and demanded more money. He said Laiba had been in severe distress for five to six days before her death and blamed Noman and Aiza for her suffering.A separate complaint lodged by Laiba's uncle, Amjad Rehman, with the FIA's Anti-Human Trafficking Circle named Noman and Aiza as accused in an alleged conspiracy to defraud the family of Rs 9.3 million. The complaint alleged that Rs 2.9 million was transferred to Noman's bank account, while the remaining amount was paid in cash at a shop in Gulistan Plaza, G-10 Markaz.Senior lawyer Raja Naveed Kiyani said police and the FIA could register separate FIRs over the same incident. He explained that the FIA could pursue its own investigation and seek Noman's custody through the court after he was transferred from police custody to judicial remand.The allegations against Noman and Aiza are yet to be established in court. The case has also highlighted concerns over fraudulent educational consultants who target Pakistani students seeking admission and scholarships abroad.
Article Summary: 20-year-old physics gold medallist committed suicide after allegedly being scammed of Pakistani Rs 93 lakh over promise of getting an admission in Harvard. An Islamabad court on Monday granted police five days of physical remand of the main accused, Muhammad Noman, in connection with the case.

Article Title: Imran Khan’s stronghold in crisis: What's happening after emergency rule in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Article Text:
Supporters of imprisoned former Pak PM Imran Khan's at protest to condemn state of emergency in northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province

Why governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa?

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa apex committee vows continued operations

Imran Khan’s son condemns emergency

Petition challenges emergency and governor’s rule in court

Roadblocks, arrests and school closures

Why Khyber Pakhtunkhwa is important to Imran Khan’s PTI

What now

Pakistan’s political confrontation over jailed former prime minister Imran Khan has escalated after the federal government imposed emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, suspending the authority of the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI)-led provincial administration. The move, announced on Sunday, brings one of the party’s most important political strongholds under federal control and has intensified tensions between the government led by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Khan’s supporters.President Asif Ali Zardari approved the measures under Articles 232(1) and 234(1) of Pakistan’s Constitution, citing a deteriorating security situation. Islamabad has accused the provincial government of failing to cooperate in the fight against terrorism, while the PTI has called the move an attempt to undermine its electoral mandate. A petition challenging the measures was filed in the Peshawar high court on Monday. Meanwhile, arrests, roadblocks, school closures and examination postponements have disrupted life in several districts as the authorities tighten security.The federal government announced emergency and governor’s rule after a cabinet meeting on Sunday reviewed the security situation in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which borders Afghanistan and has faced a persistent militant threat.In a statement, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s office said the cabinet had examined the deteriorating law and order situation and the provincial government’s “deliberate indifference in the war against terrorism”.Islamabad has accused the PTI-led administration of failing to take adequate action against militants and of not cooperating with federal authorities on security policy. Federal ministers have also alleged a “nexus” between the provincial government and terrorist groups, a charge the PTI disputes.Militants linked to Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which shares an ideological affinity with the Afghan Taliban, have carried out attacks against security personnel and civilians in Pakistan. The federal government has argued that a coordinated response is necessary to counter the threat.The PTI, however, says it has been excluded from decisions concerning security in its own province. It has opposed military operations on its territory and called for a review of the counterterrorism strategy, including Islamabad’s approach to engagement with the Afghan Taliban.The disagreement contributed to the breakdown of talks between the federal government and PTI representatives on October 3.Under governor’s rule, Governor Faisal Karim Kundi has taken charge of running the province. The federal government has also authorised the deployment of Pakistan Army troops and assets in aid of civil power.The federal government has cited worsening law and order as the basis for its intervention. However, figures from the Islamabad-based Centre for Research and Security Studies (CRSS), cited in the morning report, suggest the trend in reported deaths in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was not identical to the national picture.Civilian and security personnel deaths in the province reportedly totalled 485 in the first nine months of 2026, a decline of 16 per cent from the same period in 2025. Across Pakistan, such deaths rose by 9 per cent over the corresponding period, according to the think-tank.The figures provide a counterpoint to the federal government’s account of the province’s security situation, but they do not, by themselves, establish whether the provincial administration adequately addressed militant activity or explain the reasons behind the change in fatalities.The new administration has pledged to strengthen the police and the Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD), increase operational resources and continue intelligence-based operations against militants.The provincial Apex Committee held its first meeting under the new arrangement on Monday at the Governor House in Peshawar. It was co-chaired by Kundi and interior minister Mohsin Naqvi and attended by senior civil and military officials, including the Peshawar Corps Commander, chief secretary and inspector general of police.Kundi said tackling terrorism would be the administration’s immediate priority, pointing to what he described as a lack of coordination in counterterrorism efforts. “We can sacrifice our development, but never security,” he said, adding that the administration would “fulfil the demands of the Counter-Terrorism Department and police”, reported Dawn.He also promised a more results-oriented approach. “We have to show the difference,” Kundi said, adding that the administration would “work 24/7”.The governor highlighted the impact of militancy on daily life in districts such as Dera Ismail Khan, Tank and Waziristan, saying residents faced restrictions on their freedom to live and travel. He called for restoring normal movement and expressed hope that the new administration would be remembered for bringing peace to the province.Naqvi, meanwhile, accused the previous provincial government of failing to lead the fight against terrorism despite repeated requests from the Centre. “Today is the first time I can proudly say that the federal and the provincial governments are on the same page,” he said.Naqvi argued that security operations could not succeed without political leadership. “But any war, no matter how many resources you have, cannot be won until the government leads it,” he said.He cautioned that the situation would not change overnight but called on the governor, police, administration and federal government to work together.The committee resolved to continue intelligence-based operations and use all available resources to improve law and order. It also decided to strengthen the police and CTD with modern equipment, vehicles, armoured vehicles, weapons and additional personnel.Alongside security, the committee pledged to address public grievances, improve access to basic services and promote development in underdeveloped and conflict-affected areas.Kasim Khan, son of the jailed former prime minister, condemned the emergency and governor’s rule, accusing Army Chief Asim Munir of using terrorism as a justification for another military operation in Pashtun areas.In a post on X, Kasim linked the measures to protests demanding his father’s release and alleged that the authorities were seeking to consolidate power through military action.“Pakistan belongs to its people, not its military,” he wrote.Kasim called for the restoration of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s democratic mandate and the immediate release of his father, detained family members, PTI representatives and other political prisoners. He also demanded that the right to protest be respected.The emergency was imposed as the PTI was holding a long march led by provincial Chief Minister Sohail Afridi. The march called for Imran Khan’s release and access to medical treatment for him, while also opposing military operations that the party says have caused civilian deaths and damage.Afridi and seven other PTI leaders were taken into protective custody, according to reports. Afridi had vowed to continue the march before the provincial government’s powers were suspended, PTI reported.“There is no option other than accepting our demands,” Afridi said in a post on X before the takeover.“We will not back down,” he added. “Our long march will continue until the demands are met, in accordance with the law. Here, only Imran Khan’s policy will prevail.”The PTI has accused the federal government of using security concerns to weaken the party and undermine the elected provincial administration.“The arrest of chief minister Sohail Afridi and Junaid Akbar has exposed the political nature of the government’s actions,” PTI spokesperson Sheikh Waqas Akram said in a statement.“These measures are not directed at addressing security challenges; they are intended to weaken PTI, undermine the elected government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and disregard the democratic will of its people,” he alleged.The status of Junaid Akbar, a member of parliament and president of the PTI’s provincial chapter, requires separate confirmation before any arrest claim is treated as established.The federal government’s decision faced a legal challenge on Monday, with a petition filed in the Peshawar High Court less than 24 hours after the measures were introduced.Filed by Advocate Salman, the petition names President Zardari, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Governor Kundi as respondents. It argues that the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule is “unconstitutional, illegal and motivated by mala fide intentions”.The petitioner has also alleged that the measures violate fundamental rights and undermine the democratic mandate of the people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.Separately, opposition leaders met in Islamabad on Monday to discuss the emergency and its aftermath. Those present included PTI chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan, National Assembly Opposition Leader Mahmood Khan Achakzai and PTI secretary general Barrister Salman Akram Raja. The participants also discussed challenging the measures in court.The legal challenge adds another front to the confrontation, with the province’s administrative status now under scrutiny alongside the government’s security justification.The impact of the emergency has varied across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, with heightened security deployments, transport restrictions, school closures and arrests reported in several districts.In Peshawar, police remained deployed along major roads, while shipping containers blocked several routes, particularly around the cantonment area. Entry and exit points to Peshawar Cantt were closed, and access to areas including Khyber Road, parts of University Road and GT Road near Pir Zakori was restricted. Commuters were diverted to alternative routes.Traffic was relatively light on parts of the city’s road network on Monday afternoon. Educational institutions across the provincial capital remained closed. Internet and cellular services, which had been disrupted, were reported to have been fully restored in Peshawar, according to Dawn News.In Mardan, government and private schools, colleges and universities were shut, and examinations scheduled for the day were cancelled. Several education boards postponed secondary school examinations, including in Bannu, North Waziristan, Dera Ismail Khan and Lakki Marwat. Fresh dates are to be announced.In Charsadda, police confirmed that 15 PTI workers had been arrested. In Shangla, more than two dozen party workers had been taken into custody, according to the district police chief. Authorities also imposed Section 144, prohibiting gatherings, and ordered intensified patrolling and checks at district entry and exit points.Containers were placed to block the Islamabad-Peshawar Motorway near Swabi, where internet and mobile services remained suspended. In Bannu, road restrictions were reported near the cantonment area.The situation was comparatively calm in parts of Khyber district. A PTI demonstration in Bara was dispersed by police, but roads, including the main Peshawar-Torkham Highway, remained open.In Lower South Waziristan, schools and colleges were closed, but markets and routine commercial activities continued. No major disruption to commercial activity or significant protests were reported there.Tank district imposed a one-month ban on pillion riding from October 10 to November 9 under Section 144, citing security concerns.The differing conditions across districts underline the uneven impact of the emergency. While restrictions have affected transport, education and political activity in several areas, routine life has continued in others.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has been a key political base for Imran Khan’s PTI, which has governed the province since 2013. The party remained a major force in the 2024 elections despite Khan’s imprisonment and the difficulties faced by its candidates.Khan, a former Pakistan cricket captain who served as prime minister from 2018 to 2022, was removed from office through a parliamentary no-confidence vote. He has been in Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi since 2023 and faces more than 100 cases, including corruption and charges related to inciting violence.Candidates backed by Khan won the largest number of seats in the National Assembly in the 2024 elections, but the party was kept out of federal power as other political parties formed the government.The takeover of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa therefore carries significance beyond the change in provincial administration. It places a crucial PTI-governed province under a federal arrangement at a time when the party is mobilising supporters for Khan’s release and challenging Islamabad’s counterterrorism policy.The PTI maintains that the federal government’s actions undermine the provincial electorate’s mandate. Islamabad, in turn, argues that the security situation requires decisive intervention and closer coordination between the provincial and federal authorities.The imposition of governor’s rule has sharpened the divide between the PML-N-led federal government and the PTI, which has governed Khyber Pakhtunkhwa for more than a decade. Their dispute centres on responsibility for worsening militancy, the scope of military operations and the provincial administration’s role in security policymaking.The Centre maintains that the provincial government failed to adequately support counterterrorism efforts. The PTI says it was excluded from decisions concerning its own province and argues that the takeover undermines the democratic mandate of its voters.With the emergency facing a legal challenge, PTI leaders in custody and security restrictions disrupting parts of the province, the confrontation is now unfolding on political, judicial and security fronts. The federal government has pledged a more coordinated campaign against terrorism, while the opposition is demanding the restoration of the province’s elected administration.
Article Summary: The federal government has imposed emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, suspending the authority of the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI)-led provincial administration. Islamabad has accused the provincial government of failing to cooperate in the fight against terrorism. A petition challenging the measures was filed in the Peshawar high court on Monday.

Article Title: Why did Pakistan declare Emergency in Imran Khan's bastion Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Article Text:
Emergency in Imran Khan’s bastion: Why Shehbaz Sharif’s govt took control of KP

PTI leaders arrested after emergency announcement

Imran Khan’s stronghold at the centre of political battle

Pakistan's political battle with jailed former prime minister Imran Khan has taken a sharp turn, with the Shehbaz Sharif government suspending his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI)-led administration in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and imposing governor's rule in the province.The move brings one of Imran Khan's strongest political strongholds under direct control of the Shehbaz Sharif-led government, further deepening the confrontation between the military-backed government and PTI.Amid growing insecurities within the Shehbaz Sharif-Asim Munir duo, Imran Khan’s party has lost control of a province with around 40 million people, turning the region into the latest flashpoint in Pakistan’s political unrest.Thousands of people have taken to the streets in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa since early October, demanding Imran Khan’s release and protesting the military’s counter-insurgency operations along the border with Afghanistan.The Pakistan government has defended the move, citing the worsening law and order situation and accusing the provincial administration of failing to act against terrorism. Militants linked to Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), an ideological ally of the Afghan Taliban, have killed thousands of security personnel and civilians in recent years.“The Cabinet took a detailed review of the deteriorating law and order situation in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the circumstances arising from the provincial government’s deliberate indifference in the war against terrorism,” the office of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said in a statement.However, figures compiled by the Islamabad-based Centre for Research and Security Studies (CRSS) paint a different picture of the security situation in the province, as Financial Times reported.Civilian and security personnel deaths in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa stood at 485 in the first nine months of 2026, down 16% from the same period in 2025. Across Pakistan, such deaths rose by 9%, according to the think-tank.Pakistan President Asif Ali Zardari approved the emergency on the prime minister’s advice. His office cited a “failure of negotiations” between the Pakistan government and PTI leaders in the province.Under governor’s rule, the governor, who is appointed by the Pakistan government, takes over the province’s administration. Pakistan’s interior ministry said the army would deploy personnel to help run the province and protect public property and government installations.Talal Chaudhry, junior interior minister, told the Financial Times that the move was a “routine measure” intended to help provincial authorities carry out their responsibilities, particularly in the fight against terrorism.The political confrontation intensified soon after the announcement, with reports emerging that senior PTI leaders had been arrested.An account on X associated with Junaid Akbar, a member of parliament and president of PTI’s provincial chapter, said he and provincial chief minister Sohail Afridi had been taken into custody.Afridi, 37, had been leading a long march across the province in support of Khan and against military operations that PTI claims have caused civilian deaths and damage. He is the youngest-ever chief minister of Pakistan and comes from the tribal belt bordering Afghanistan.Just hours before his government was suspended, Afridi had vowed to continue the march until the protesters’ demands were met.“There is no option other than accepting our demands,” Afridi said in a post on X.“We will not back down,” he said. “Our long march will continue until the demands are met, in accordance with the law. Here, only Imran Khan’s policy will prevail.”Pakistan’s interior ministry and armed forces did not respond to requests for comment, the Financial Times reported.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has been a key political base for Imran Khan's PTI, which has governed the province since 2013. The party won more than 60% of the seats in the provincial assembly in the 2024 elections, two years after Khan was removed as prime minister through a parliamentary no-confidence vote.The former World Cup-winning cricket captain continues to be widely regarded as Pakistan’s most popular politician. Candidates backed by him won the largest number of seats in the national assembly in 2024.However, they were kept out of power as the military and the country’s two dominant dynastic political parties shaped the post-election arrangement, according to the Financial Times.The FT also cited analysts as saying PTI would comfortably win a competitive general election.PTI has accused the Shehbaz Sharif government of using security concerns as a pretext to remove its elected administration in the province.“The arrest of chief minister Sohail Afridi and Junaid Akbar has exposed the political nature of the government’s actions,” PTI spokesperson Sheikh Waqas Akram said in a statement.“These measures are not directed at addressing security challenges; they are intended to weaken PTI, undermine the elected government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and disregard the democratic will of its people.”
Article Summary: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa is one of Imran Khan's strongest political strongholds. Shehbaz Sharif-led government has imposed governor's rule in the province. Reports emerge that senior PTI leaders have been arrested. Pakistan government has defended the move, citing the worsening law and order situation.

Article Title: Pak crisis: Shehbaz govt declares emergency, ends Imran Khan's party's rule in KPK
Article Text:
PTI has been mobilising supporters to pressure the federal government over Khan's imprisonment

Terrorism, law and order cited

PTI protests, warns of bloodshed

Pakistan on Sunday declared an emergency in northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KPK), suspending the provincial government led by jailed former prime minister Imran Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party amid deteriorating law and order and a growing confrontation with Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's government.President Asif Ali Zardari issued the proclamation under Articles 232(1) and 234(1) of the Constitution, citing rising terrorist attacks and a breakdown of constitutional machinery in the province. The move strips the elected provincial administration of its powers, with the chief minister, provincial ministers, advisers, special assistants and advocate general required to vacate their offices.Following the announcement the Pak government order the deployment of army in the province.The decision comes as thousands of PTI supporters march towards Islamabad, demanding Khan's release and access to medical treatment for the former prime minister, who has been in prison since 2023 on corruption and other charges. The party has described the cases against him as politically motivated. The emergency also follows failed negotiations between PTI and the federal government over the planned protest.The presidential declaration said the emergency had been imposed because of the grave security situation and the provincial government's alleged failure to tackle militancy.“The extraordinary intensity of terrorist incidents poses serious threats to the lives and property of the public,” the declaration stated.PTI has been mobilising supporters to pressure the federal government over Khan's imprisonment. KPK chief minister Sohail Afridi is leading the protest march, which began in Lakki Marwat on October 4 and has passed through several districts.The party had initially planned to take the march to Islamabad for a sit-in, but authorities have erected roadblocks using shipping containers at entry points to the capital and other locations.
